opening.headline: Draw a line in the agent architecture that separates the believed region from the unbelieved region, and assess the risk of data that lies beyond this line.
body: The diagram shows users, web apps, orchestrators, model APIs, search repositories, web browser tools, and on-premises databases as boxes connected by arrows. However, no line indicates which side represents the trusted path and which represents the untrusted path. Therefore, it is impossible to determine where data should be inspected.

In this class, we first confirm what to draw in a data flow diagram and examine why the trust boundary line indicates potential attack points. Then, we draw five boundaries on an agent architecture diagram and learn how to assess the risk of data crossing these boundaries using two criteria.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: You can identify the confidence boundaries in a configuration.
Can assess the risks of data flows crossing boundaries

screens.title: There is structure, but no boundaries are visible.
screens.lead: Read the following scene and think about what you are immersed in. The dashed question mark in the diagram represents a line that has not yet been drawn.

visual.alt: A diagram of an agent composition showing only boxes and arrows, with a boundary line indicated by a question mark.
labels: Dot punctuation mark = the boundary of faith yet to be determined

paragraphs: The team drew the agent architecture. The user connects to a web app, the orchestrator calls a model API, and the search repository, web browser tool, and on-premises database are connected. All components are present, and the arrows are accurate.

However, this single diagram does not indicate which line represents the side of belief and which side represents disbelief. Since all boxes have the same shape and color, database records and web pages from the internet appear to have the same weight. Without any basis, we cannot determine where verification is required.
The question for this class is this: How do we find and draw the confidence boundary from a diagram, and how do we determine when data exceeds that boundary?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Topology shows what is connected, but it does not indicate whom to trust. The boundaries of trust must be added through analysis.

screens.outro: First, let's recall what we believe and what we do not believe based on the current configuration.

screens.title: Believing and not believing
screens.lead: When a question is selected, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. There is no input or submission field, so first take a moment to reflect on your own system.

items.prompt: Have you ever distinguished between what you believe and what you do not believe in a configuration?
items.answer: Typically, components are treated as having equal weight without distinction. When differentiated, we see a separation between the parts that our team creates and manages, and those parts contributed by external sources. This boundary is therefore a candidate for the trust boundary.

items.prompt: Who can create and who can edit documents in the search repository?
items.answer: Just because it's an internal repository doesn't mean it's secure. If many employees can edit content through collaboration tools or if external documents are automatically collected, the content within the repository becomes authored by diverse individuals. Whether the content is trustworthy depends not on whether it's internal, but on who can create and edit it.

items.prompt: Can the page retrieved by the web browser tool be considered trustworthy content?
items.answer: It's safer to assume something is not trustworthy. Since we cannot control what the page owner has configured. This is precisely why we need to draw a line at the point where this text enters the model context.

screens.outro: Now I'll summarize what boundaries do in a data flow diagram.

screens.title: Data Flow Diagram and Trust Boundary
screens.lead: Each row in the table describes one element to be drawn in a data flow diagram. Compare the element to the corresponding agent in the agent diagram to determine what it represents.

data.caption: Example of elements drawn in a data flow diagram (DFD) and an agent configuration diagram
rows: A person or service that interacts with the system from outside the system
Internet users, external MCP servers, third-party websites
A component that receives data, processes it, and then passes it on.
Web app, Orchestrate, Model API call, Tool executor
Search repository, internal database, chat logs
User query, search results, model output, tool call request and result
A line indicating areas with different confidence levels
Between the internet and web apps, between external content and model context, between model output and tool execution
data.notes: OWASP explains that a system model must clearly illustrate trust boundaries, data flows, data stores, processes, and external entities. These elements are commonly attack surfaces and serve as inputs for the subsequent threat identification phase. For complex systems, a high-level overview diagram combined with detailed component diagrams is maintained in a form that the team can easily modify. In LLM agents, a single model context is represented as one process, but by adding annotations to the diagram indicating the presence of system prompts, user inputs, and external content within that process, it becomes helpful for later threat identification. Furthermore, all five elements of the table must be illustrated to clearly define which flow each boundary governs. The diagrams should be updated continuously—not finalized once—and revised whenever new tools or data sources are added.

screens.outro: Having verified the elements, we'll now directly draw boundaries on the agent configuration above.

screens.title: Draw boundaries on agent topology
screens.lead: When a boundary marker number on the diagram is selected, a description for that boundary will open. Check what data crosses each boundary.

visual.alt: Five dashed boundaries with numbered markers are drawn on the agent schema diagram.
labels: Commands and data in the same text

markers.label: User and web app
markers.title: Boundary 1: From the Internet to our web application
markers.body: This is the most familiar boundary. Traditional web security measures such as authentication and input validation are present here. However, merely drawing this single boundary would make all internal events appear as if they were trusted; therefore, the internal boundaries below must also be drawn together.

markers.label: External text and context
markers.title: Boundary 2: Search repository·web page as model context
markers.body: This is a place where the author of the retrieved text might not be part of our team. Text entering beyond this line is seen by the model as identical characters to the user's original message. This boundary should be considered first in terms of source attribution and content verification.

markers.label: Model output and tools
markers.title: Boundary 3: From model output to tool execution
markers.body: This is the point where the model-defined call transforms into actual behavior. On the line's left side are text elements, while on the right side are effects such as email transmission or data modification. Actions with high impact can require approval at this boundary.

markers.label: Tools and External Systems
markers.title: Boundary 4: From internal DB to tools and external services
markers.body: This is where permissions are defined. Here, it is determined whether a tool connects using a specific account, and whether it is granted only read access or also write access. Even if defenses are breached at Boundary 2, if the permissions at this boundary are restrictive, the impact can be minimized.

markers.label: MCP Server
markers.title: Boundary 5: From external MCP server to agent
markers.body: Tool descriptions and execution results are provided externally. Description texts, being input data read by the model, must be treated as out-of-bounds data. We define how much we trust the server provider and document the trusted scope.

screens.outro: Within a model context, remember that it can be difficult to draw a line between instructions and data when they are both presented as the same text.

screens.title: Risk assessment of data crossing boundaries
screens.lead: Compare how risk changes by alternately selecting between two states. The two criteria for risk assessment are whether the source can be controlled and whether permissions exist at the location where data is accessed.

states.label: When the source can be controlled
states.body: For example, this is the flow of searching for policy documents that our team has authored and maintains change history. Since we know both the author and the scope of modifications, the risk is relatively low. That said, because the data crosses boundaries, it remains within the scope of inspection. There is still a need for an approval step if any tool with write permissions accesses it.

states.label: When the source cannot be controlled
states.body: This occurs when search results or external wiki content follow the same flow. The author cannot be identified, and the content may change at any time, making it high-risk. If this data reaches read-only tools only, the impact is limited; however, if it reaches tools with write permissions in the ticketing system, it becomes one of the most dangerous pathways. This pathway first includes review and approval steps. The judgment can be easily understood as the product of two criteria: the less familiar the source, the higher the priority when permissions are high. Conversely, if the source is well-known but the data reaches locations with write and delete permissions, approval procedures are not bypassed. The core of this judgment lies in the fact that the level of required controls varies depending on where the data reaches.

screens.outro: We have established the criteria; now let's follow a specific example case through its path as an explanation.

screens.title: Explanation: Web search results as the pathway that triggers tool calls
screens.lead: The instructor demonstrates stepping through one path in boundary order. Press the start button and advance one step at a time using the arrow, and verify the checks available at each boundary.

steps.title: Scenario: Agent that searches and comments on tickets
steps.body: The agent has a tool that reads and summarizes web search results to post comments in a ticketing system. The diagram contains only a few boxes and arrows, making it unclear where risks might lie. We will now overlay this flow on top of the previously outlined boundaries.

steps.title: Step 1: The search body exceeds boundary 2
steps.body: The search result body is loaded into the model context. The source cannot be controlled, and the text may contain statements directed at the model. Within this boundary, possible actions include providing source attribution, checking for known hazardous phrases, and delivering the body content as mere material rather than as instructions.

steps.title: Step 2: The hidden sentence is integrated into the plan
steps.body: The model cannot perfectly distinguish between sentences in the main text and reference materials or instructions. Therefore, if a sentence in the main text specifies writing certain content, it may be mixed into the model's tool-calling plan. This step occurs internally within the model, making it impossible to draw a clear boundary directly.

steps.title: Step 3: The model output exceeds boundary 3
steps.body: When the model creates a comment composition call, its output is passed to the tool executor. At the moment the text becomes an action, the call parameters are checked, and significant calls require human approval.

steps.title: Step 4: Encounters write permission at Boundary 4
steps.body: The tool has permission to write in the ticket system. The wider this permission, the greater the potential damage if the initial defenses are breached. By narrowing the permissions so that the tool can only post comments but cannot delete or modify entries, the scope of potential damage is reduced.

steps.title: Conclusion: The most dangerous path
steps.body: The most dangerous path in this architecture is the flow that reaches writable tools from an uncontrollable source. Defenses should be built in this order: place checks and approvals at boundaries 2 and 3, and reduce privileges at boundary 4. Only by doing so can the priority of defenses be properly explained.

screens.outro: With boundaries established, we can now describe risks. Let me summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaways
screens.lead: Think about taking the first step to define the core of the lesson and establish boundaries within your architecture.

paragraphs: All data crossing boundaries is subject to inspection. The trust boundary is drawn at points in the data flow where trust levels differ. This boundary exists not only between the internet and web applications, but also between external inputs and model context, between model outputs and tools, and between tools and external systems.

Risk is assessed by considering two factors together: whether we control the source, and what permissions the data has when it reaches certain locations. The most dangerous path is when a source we cannot control flows through a location with high permissions, and defense is built against such paths. As SAIF states, AI risk must be understood within the context of the surrounding workflow processes.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Boundaries are not pre-drawn on a configuration diagram. Boundaries are lines added analytically on top of the configuration diagram and must be updated together with the system.

glossary.def: This line represents the confidence level that separates different regions. Data exceeding this line is subject to inspection.
This is a diagram illustrating processes, data repositories, external entities, data flows, and boundaries. It is a representative tool answering the first question in threat modeling.
This refers to data crossing a trust boundary into a region with a different trust level.
This is a flow wherein data from an uncontrollable source reaches a location with high privileges.

misconceptions.myth: If a configuration is present, the trust boundary is already displayed.
misconceptions.fact: A configuration typically consists of boxes and lines. Information on where the trusted region begins must be added through analysis.

misconceptions.myth: The trust boundary is the one thing between the Internet and our web app.
misconceptions.fact: There are boundaries not only between search documents and model context, but also between model output and tools, and between tools and external systems.

misconceptions.myth: Documents in the internal repository are always trustworthy.
misconceptions.fact: The trustworthiness varies depending on who can use and modify it, even if the repository is on-premises.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: All data crossing the boundary is subject to inspection.
Drawing a trust boundary on a data flow diagram reveals potential attack points.
Identifies the most dangerous paths based on source control feasibility and reachability permissions.
The point where a model's output transitions into a tool must be considered a boundary.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: In our architecture, where should the trust boundary be placed, and what is the most dangerous data that crosses beyond that boundary?

title: Reading trust boundaries and architecture diagrams

checks.q: Pair the boundaries of the agent architecture with notable points at those boundaries.
left: Search repository · web pages ↔ model context
right: Tool description and results are provided from external sources.
This is where permissions are defined.
The model-defined call becomes an actual action.
The person who wrote the content might not be from our team.
checks.explain: The context boundary may be external, the model output boundary is triggered by an action, and permissions are defined at the tool and DB boundary. The MCP boundary has tool descriptions and results coming from outside.
checks.intro: Pair the boundaries of composition and notable points at those boundaries. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: I have correctly connected all features of the boundary.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Some connections are out of sync. Review again what is defined between the tool and the database.

checks.q: What is an appropriate reason to consider the most dangerous path in an agent that reads web search results and posts comments to a ticket system?
options: The search results are long, leading to high context costs.
The fact that internet users connect to web applications
The fact that data whose source cannot be controlled reaches tools with write permissions
The data flow diagram is represented as a single overview diagram.
checks.explain: Risk arises when uncontrolled data encounters permissions at the locations it reaches. This refers to the flow where uncontrolled search content leads into write-permission tools.

wrong.0: Cost is not the axis for judging the risk of a path.
wrong.1: User connectivity is the most familiar boundary, but it is not the most dangerous pathway.
wrong.3: The composition style of the image is independent of the path's risk level.

checks.intro: For the agent case used in the ticket system, consider selecting evidence for risk assessment. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes, that's correct. This judgment considers both source control and access permissions.
checks.incorrectFeedback: You selected criteria unrelated to risk, such as cost or connection path. Please review your two judgment criteria again.
